name: Fortezza of Rethymno
architectural_style: One of the largest Venetian fortresses ever built; pentagonal circuit of massive bastions and curtain walls on the Palaiokastro promontory above Rethymno; designed by Sforza Pallavicini following the Ottoman sack of Rethymno in 1571; the Ibrahim Han mosque (converted from the Cathedral of St. Nicholas) is the dominant surviving interior structure

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Open daily in season (April–October); winter hours shorter. The GYG guided tour (t1233980) includes entrance ticket and skip-the-line access.

accessibility: The Fortezza is on a promontory above Rethymno old town; the main entrance is reached by a moderate uphill walk from the harbour area (10–15 minutes). The interior is largely flat once inside the walls. The GYG tour meets at the fortress entrance.
tagline: One of the largest Venetian fortresses ever built — the 16th-century bastion above Rethymno's old town that the Venetians built after Ottoman raiders burned the city, and the Ottomans took anyway
highlights: One of the largest Venetian fortresses in the world — the Fortezza's pentagonal circuit of massive bastions and curtain walls, built from 1573 on the natural promontory above Rethymno, encloses an area large enough to shelter the entire population of the city in the event of attack; the scale is extraordinary even by the standards of Venetian military engineering

Built after catastrophe — the Ottoman fleet sacked Rethymno in 1571 and carried off 3,000 inhabitants into slavery; the Fortezza was the Venetian Republic's direct response, intended to prevent it happening again. It did not: the Ottomans took the fortress in 1646

The Ibrahim Han mosque — inside the fortress, the largest surviving structure is the mosque converted from the Venetian Cathedral of St. Nicholas. Its dome and minaret visible above the fortress walls are the most striking silhouette of the Fortezza when seen from Rethymno's harbour

Entrance included with skip-the-line access — the GYG guided tour of Rethymno (t1233980, from €55, 1 review) includes the Fortezza entrance ticket and skip-the-line access, with a certified local guide; this is the most assured way to experience the fortress with expert commentary on its construction and history

Rethymno old town — directly below the Fortezza, one of the best-preserved Venetian old towns in Greece, with minarets, Venetian loggia, and fountain surviving from 400 years of Venetian and Ottoman rule
description:
The Fortezza of Rethymno was built in anger. In 1571 — the same year as the Battle of Lepanto — an Ottoman fleet descended on Rethymno, sacked the city, and carried approximately 3,000 of its inhabitants into slavery. The Venetian Republic, which administered Rethymno as part of its Cretan possessions, responded with a construction programme of exceptional ambition: a fortress on the Palaiokastro promontory above the city so large that it could shelter the entire urban population within its walls in the event of another attack.

Designed by the Venetian military engineer Sforza Pallavicini and constructed from 1573, the Fortezza is among the largest Venetian fortresses ever built. The pentagonal circuit of bastions and curtain walls encloses an area of approximately 40,000 square metres — large enough to have contained a mini-city within the fortress, complete with barracks, storehouses, churches, a lighthouse, and cisterns. The construction used local limestone and incorporated the natural topography of the promontory to maximise the defensive advantage of the cliff-edge position.

It did not save Rethymno. Ottoman forces invested the Fortezza in 1646 during their campaign to take Crete, and the city fell that same year. The fortress was held by Ottoman forces for the following 254 years, until Crete's union with Greece in 1913. The most visible trace of the Ottoman period inside the fortress is the Ibrahim Han mosque, converted from the Venetian Cathedral of St. Nicholas — its dome and minaret dominate the interior skyline and are visible from the harbour below.

The GYG guided tour of Rethymno (t1233980) includes the Fortezza entrance ticket and skip-the-line access with a certified local guide. Entrance is confirmed included in the tour price — this is one of the few Crete fortress experiences where the entry fee is genuinely bundled into the GYG tour cost. After the fortress, the same guide covers Rethymno's old town, with its Venetian loggia, the Rimondi Fountain, and the minarets that give the town its distinctive layered heritage character.
history: Rethymno was a Venetian-administered city from 1204, when the Fourth Crusade's aftermath delivered Crete to the Republic of Venice. The promontory above the city (Palaiokastro) had a small medieval fortification before the Fortezza, but the 1571 Ottoman sack made a far larger defensive programme unavoidable. Construction began in 1573 under Sforza Pallavicini and continued for several decades. The Ottomans besieged the Fortezza in 1646 as part of their campaign to capture Crete (the main campaign began in 1645); the fortress surrendered and Rethymno became an Ottoman city. During the Ottoman period, the Cathedral of St. Nicholas inside the fortress was converted to the Ibrahim Han mosque. Crete's incorporation into the Greek state was completed in 1913. The Fortezza has been open to visitors as a heritage site since the 20th century; the Ibrahim Han mosque, though not in religious use, is preserved within the site.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Rethymno is on Crete's northern coast, approximately 80 km west of Heraklion and 60 km east of Chania — accessible by bus on the national coastal highway (2 hours from Heraklion, 1.5 hours from Chania). The Fortezza is at the northern end of the old town, a 15-minute uphill walk from the Venetian harbour. The GYG tour meets at the fortress entrance.

**Tickets:** Walk-up entry is approximately €6 per adult; children (typically under 18 with ID) enter free. The GYG certified guided tour of Rethymno (t1233980, from €55 per person, 1 review so far) includes the Fortezza entrance ticket and skip-the-line access, with a certified local guide for the fortress and old town. Entry is confirmed included — no additional cost at the fortress gate.

**Practical tips:** Visit the Fortezza in the late afternoon when the light on the bastions is best and the heat has reduced; the fortress is fully exposed and can be extremely hot at midday in July and August. The Ibrahim Han mosque is the most photogenic interior feature — approach it from the main path through the fortress. After the fortress, walk down through the old town to the Venetian harbour for the best views back up at the Fortezza from the water.

**Combine with:** [Spinalonga Island Fortress](/castles/greece/spinalonga-island-fortress) (~150 km east on Crete's northeastern coast — the 1579 Venetian island fortress and former leper colony in the Gulf of Elounda; note: €20 entry paid on-site) and [Palace of the Grand Master](/castles/greece/palace-of-the-grand-master) (~300 km east on Rhodes — the 14th-century Knights Hospitaller palace in Rhodes's walled old town, with a different perspective on Aegean medieval military heritage).

faqs.question: How large is the Fortezza of Rethymno, and was it really large enough to shelter the whole city?
faqs.answer: The Fortezza encloses approximately 40,000 square metres — a very large area for a Venetian-era fortress. The Venetian Republic's design brief was explicitly to build a fortress large enough to shelter the entire population of Rethymno (at the time a city of several thousand) inside its walls during an Ottoman naval attack. The interior plan included barracks for troops, storehouses for provisions, cisterns for water, and space for the civilian population. Whether it could have achieved this in practice during a sustained siege is a different question — but the design intent was genuine, and the scale reflects the Venetian Republic's determination after the 1571 disaster.

faqs.question: What is the Ibrahim Han mosque inside the fortress, and can you go inside?
faqs.answer: The Ibrahim Han mosque is the Ottoman conversion of the Venetian Cathedral of St. Nicholas, built inside the Fortezza during the Venetian period and converted to Islamic use after the Ottoman conquest in 1646. The dome and minaret were added during the conversion. The structure is the most prominent building inside the fortress walls. In recent decades, the building has been used as an archaeological display space during some periods; access and interior opening may vary. The exterior and the relationship of the dome and minaret to the surrounding Venetian walls is in any case the most photographed view inside the Fortezza.

faqs.question: If the Venetian Republic built such a massive fortress, why did the Ottomans take it so quickly in 1646?
faqs.answer: The Fortezza fell in 1646 primarily because the Ottoman besieging force was very large and the Venetian garrison defending it was small and undersupplied. The Venetian Republic's ability to resupply and reinforce Crete was limited by the scale of the Ottoman naval commitment to the Cretan campaign. The Fortezza's design was excellent and would have been capable of sustained resistance if properly garrisoned — but the garrison was not adequate for a prolonged siege against the resources the Ottomans brought to bear. The defence lasted several months before surrender; the fall of Rethymno was not an indictment of the fortress design but of the broader Venetian strategic situation.
